title: Cleaning and polishing a verdigris brass fitting
subtitle: Remove the green patina from a lacquered or unlacquered brass door fitting or drawer pull and polish it back to a bright, clean surface
excerpt: How to clean verdigris and oxidation from brass door fittings, drawer pulls, and cabinet hardware. Covers removing the fitting, using a mild acid cleaner or natural acids to dissolve verdigris, polishing to a shine, and deciding whether to re-lacquer.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics (referenced, not reproduced). UK heritage property maintenance guides (open access). Traditional metalwork restoration practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: The blue-green patina that forms on copper and copper alloys (brass, bronze) when exposed to air, moisture, and organic acids. Chemically, a mixture of copper carbonates, sulfates, and chlorides. Not harmful to the underlying brass but visually distinct from polished brass. Can be removed with mild acids.

A clear protective coating applied over polished brass to prevent oxidation and maintain the shine. Factory-lacquered fittings stay bright until the lacquer deteriorates or is scratched; then the bare brass beneath oxidises faster than unlacquered brass. Lacquer must be removed completely before the brass can be polished.

if present, dissolve the verdigris with an acid soak or paste, polish, and decide whether to re-lacquer or leave unlacquered.

Unscrew or unclip the fitting from the door or drawer. Note the fixing method so it goes back correctly. If the fitting has been painted over (common in old houses with many paint layers), score around the edges with a utility knife before unscrewing to avoid tearing the paint.

If the fitting is factory-lacquered, the lacquer must come off before polishing. Soak the fitting in a 50:50 solution of acetone and methylated spirit for 10 minutes, or use a proprietary paint stripper. Scrub the loosened lacquer off with a soft brass wire brush or a toothbrush. Rinse with clean water and dry.

For light verdigris, rub with half a lemon dipped in salt: the citric acid dissolves the green film. For heavier deposits, make a paste of salt and white wine vinegar or a solution of 1 part citric acid powder (food grade) dissolved in 5 parts warm water. Leave the fitting in the soak for 10 to 30 minutes, then scrub with a toothbrush. The verdigris dissolves into the acid; rinse thoroughly and dry.

Once the verdigris is gone, polish the fitting with a proprietary brass polish (Brasso or similar) applied with a soft cloth, rubbing in circular motions. Work through progressively finer cloths. Finish with a dry cloth to buff to a shine. For intricate moulded fittings, apply the polish with a soft toothbrush to reach into the relief detail.

Bare brass will tarnish again over time. A clear brass lacquer spray keeps it bright for 2 to 3 years. For old or period hardware, leaving it bare gives a period look; the brass builds up a patina slowly, which many people prefer.

attrs.symptom: Fitting is still green after soaking in acid
attrs.cause: The verdigris layer is too thick or has mineralised deeply into the surface.
attrs.fix: Soak for longer and scrub with a brass brush. For thick green build-up, buy a verdigris remover from a hardware shop. It is stronger than kitchen acids.

attrs.symptom: Fitting re-greens within a few weeks of polishing
attrs.cause: No lacquer applied after polishing, and the fitting is in a damp location.
attrs.fix: Apply two coats of clear brass lacquer spray after polishing. Allow each coat to dry fully before applying the next.
